evidence: src/infrastructure/UserController.ts setupRoutes(): router.post('/users') reads req.body, checks `name` is present, and returns res.status(400/201).json(...). This is HTTP transport work, which belongs in infrastructure.
src/infrastructure/UserController.ts setupRoutes(): the POST handler passes creation to this.createUserUseCase.execute(name), so the business logic stays in the application layer.

src/infrastructure/UserController.ts setupRoutes(): router.get('/users') calls this.userRepository.findAll() and maps it to {id, name}. This is a thin read that skips the application layer but contains no business rules. It is borderline.
src/infrastructure/UserController.ts constructor: `new CreateUserUseCase(userRepository)` is wiring work, which is acceptable in infrastructure.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: UserController is in the infrastructure layer and acts as an Express HTTP adapter. What it does fits that role: it sets up routes, reads the request body, checks that the required `name` field is present, maps exceptions to HTTP 400, sets HTTP status codes, and turns domain entities into JSON objects for the response. The POST route hands the actual user creation to CreateUserUseCase in the application layer, so no business rules live in the controller. The `if (!name)` check only confirms the request has the field; it is not a domain invariant. Building the use case in the constructor is wiring work, which is acceptable in infrastructure. The borderline point is the GET /users handler, which calls `this.userRepository.findAll()` directly and skips the application layer. That is a trivial read with no business logic. It is inconsistent with the use-case pattern the POST route follows, but it does not place domain or application rules in this file. Whether a controller may call a repository directly is mostly a layer-dependency question, which is out of scope here. No ADR text was provided that requires every read to go through a use case.
